en: The gravitational pull of the moon causes the ocean tides in Manila Bay to rise and fall twice daily.
Water droplets roll off smooth banana leaves easily because the waxy surface creates very little friction.
The smooth, sloping sides of Mayon Volcano act as a massive natural inclined plane in the landscape.
Migrating birds use the Earth's natural magnetic field to navigate during their long flights across the Pacific.
A lightning strike over Taal Volcano is a massive natural discharge of static electricity between clouds and the ground.
A rainbow appears over Subic Bay after rain because water droplets refract and reflect sunlight into different colors.
Fruit bats flying in dark Philippine caves use sound waves to bounce off walls and find their way.
Volcanic rocks near Mount Bulusan feel hot to the touch because heat conducts directly from the magma below.
Hot springs in Tiwi, Albay exist because geothermal energy from underground magma heats the groundwater to the surface.
A Philippine crocodile's jaw acts as a natural lever to snap shut quickly on prey in freshwater swamps.
The streamlined body shape of the Philippine eagle reduces air friction, allowing it to glide smoothly.
Coconuts dropping from tall palm trees accelerate toward the ground due to the Earth's constant gravitational pull.
